known_gaps:
Poverty as a standalone NCERT chapter could not be confirmed in the current (rationalised) edition — it may have been merged or dropped in a recent syllabus revision; needs a follow-up check before treating any specific poverty-line figure as NCERT-sourced. Within History, Ryotwari system, the Santhal Rebellion, 1857/Kunwar Singh, Champaran Satyagraha, and Mauryan/Pal/Patna Kalam art are named BPSC syllabus lines not yet extracted from NCERT — worth a follow-up pass since History is now a stated priority. Geography and Science & Technology extraction has not been done yet. Trade policy, WTO, Make in India, and similarly current-policy topics are not standard NCERT content at all (NCERT textbooks don't track live government schemes) — these stay general-knowledge-graded regardless of how much NCERT extraction is done, the same way current affairs and recent statistics always will.
If useful, tell me and I'll do a second History pass covering the gaps above, plus Geography and Science & Technology.

entries.heading: Fundamental Rights (Ch. 2, "Rights in the Indian Constitution")
entries.text:
Right to Equality (Art. 14–18): "equality before law – equal protection of laws"; prohibits discrimination on "religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth"; abolishes untouchability and titles. Article 16(4) permits reservation for a "backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State."
Right to Freedom (Art. 19–22): covers "freedom of speech and expression; assemble peacefully; form associations/unions; move freely throughout the territory of India; reside and settle in any part of India; practise any profession." Article 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law" — judicially expanded to include the "right to live with human dignity, free from exploitation," and the right to shelter and livelihood. Preventive detention allows arrest without standard procedure for up to three months before board review — the text itself notes "this provision has often been misused by the government."
Right against Exploitation (Art. 23–24): prohibits "traffic in human beings and forced labour" and "employment of children in hazardous jobs" (covers historical begar/bonded labour).
Right to Freedom of Religion (Art. 25–28): "freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion"; state may restrict practice "to protect public order, morality and health" (e.g., banning sati, bigamy, human sacrifice does not violate this right).
Cultural and Educational Rights (Art. 29–30): minorities may preserve their language/culture and establish/manage their own educational institutions.
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32): lets citizens approach courts directly for rights violations — Dr. Ambedkar called this "the heart and soul of the constitution." Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari.

entries.heading: Directive Principles of State Policy (same chapter)
entries.text: Non-justiciable — "cannot be enforced by the judiciary." Three broad categories: (1) goals/objectives (welfare, social/economic/political justice, equitable resource distribution); (2) non-justiciable rights (adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, right to work, early childhood care); (3) policy guidelines (Uniform Civil Code, cottage industries, village panchayats). Real legislative implementation cited by the text: zamindari abolition, bank nationalisation, factory laws, minimum wages, mid-day meal scheme.

entries.heading: Fundamental Rights ↔ DPSP relationship
entries.text: Described as "complementary to each other" — rights constrain government action, DPSPs push affirmative action. The historical flashpoint was property rights: originally a Fundamental Right, it clashed with DPSP-driven land reform. In 1973 the Supreme Court held "the right to property was not part of the basic structure of the Constitution," and the 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from Fundamental Rights, making it a simple legal right. This dispute produced the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati case): "there are certain basic features of the Constitution and these cannot be changed by Parliament."

entries.heading: Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A)
entries.text: "Article 51A containing Fundamental Duties was inserted by the Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976" — originally 10 duties (a–j); an 11th, duty (k) — providing education to one's child aged 6–14 — was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). Covers upholding the Constitution, national service, promoting harmony, preserving culture, protecting the environment, and safeguarding public property.

entries.heading: Executive — President & Governor (Ch. 4)
entries.text: President formally holds executive power, exercised through the Council of Ministers headed by the PM: "There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall... act in accordance with such advice" — binding advice, though the President may ask for reconsideration once. Three discretionary situations: (1) sending advice back for reconsideration, (2) withholding assent to a non-Money Bill with no constitutional time limit ("pocket veto"), (3) choosing a PM when no party has a clear majority. Role is largely ceremonial otherwise. Governors are appointed by the President and hold comparatively more discretionary power at the state level.

entries.heading: Legislature — Parliament (Ch. 5)
entries.text: Functions: legislative (law-making, though "the Parliament often merely approves legislations" drafted by the executive), executive control (ensuring "the executive does not overstep its authority"), financial (controls taxation/budget), representative, and debating ("the highest forum of debate in the country"). Lok Sabha exclusively controls money bills and can remove government via no-confidence motion. Rajya Sabha cannot reject money bills but approves constitutional amendments and can alone initiate Vice-President removal — it "can criticise the government but cannot remove it." Question Hour and the no-confidence motion ("the most powerful weapon") are the key accountability tools. Anti-Defection Law (1985) prevents members from switching parties without losing their seat — critics note it has "given additional powers to the party leadership."

entries.heading: Judiciary (Ch. 6)
entries.text: Independence protected via fixed tenure, difficult removal, financial autonomy, and immunity from personal criticism. Judicial review: the Supreme Court can declare a law unconstitutional if "inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution," covering both rights violations and centre-state disputes. Public Interest Litigation (PIL), from around 1979, let citizens/organisations petition on behalf of others — landmark case Hussainara Khatoon vs. Bihar (1979), concerning Bihar undertrial prisoners held longer than their likely sentence. PIL later expanded into environmental and social concerns. Judicial activism is this proactive role; critics say it "has blurred the line of distinction between the executive and legislature on the one hand and the judiciary on the other."

entries.heading: Local Governments / Panchayati Raj (Ch. 8)
entries.text: 73rd Amendment (rural) and 74th Amendment (urban), both 1992–93, created uniform local-government structures. Three-tier Panchayati Raj: Gram Panchayat (village) → Mandal/Block/Taluka Panchayat (intermediate) → Zilla Panchayat (district). Direct elections every 5 years; one-third seats reserved for women (including chairperson posts); SC/ST reservation proportional to population. 29 subjects devolved via the Eleventh Schedule (rural) and Twelfth Schedule (urban). Real-world caveat the text itself flags: states retain discretion over actually transferring functions, and financial autonomy remains limited despite the structural reform.

entries.heading: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues (Ch. 6)
entries.text: Worker: "All those who are engaged in economic activities, in whatever capacity — high or low, are workers." Workforce: ~545 million people (2022–23), roughly two-thirds rural. Worker-population ratio: ~41–44% of population. Formal sector: all public-sector establishments plus private establishments employing 10+ hired workers. Informal sector: everything else — small enterprises, self-employed, farmers, agricultural labourers — and covers roughly 89% of India's workforce. Unemployment types: disguised (more workers than needed, common in agriculture), seasonal (agriculture's seasonal nature), and open (actively seeking, unable to find work). MGNREGA (2005) promises "100 days of guaranteed wage employment" — the flagship government employment-generation measure the chapter cites.

entries.heading: Human Capital Formation (Ch. 4)
entries.text: Human capital = turning human resources (via education, health, on-the-job training, migration, information) into productive capability, distinct from "human development," where "education and health are integral to human well-being" rather than just productivity inputs. Government education spending rose from 0.64% to 4.47% of GDP (1952–2020) against a recommended 6% target — i.e., still below the recommended level. Female adult literacy rose from 37.9% (1990) to 66% (2017–18).

entries.heading: Environment and Sustainable Development (Ch. 7)
entries.text: Sustainable development: "Development that meets the need of the present generation without compromising the ability of the future generation to meet their own needs." Covers environmental degradation, resource depletion, and India's specific challenges (air/water pollution, land degradation, deforestation).

entries.heading: Land Revenue Systems (Class 8, "Ruling the Countryside")
entries.text:
Permanent Settlement (1793): made between the East India Company and "the rajas and taluqdars," who "were recognised as zamindars." Key term: "the amount to be paid was fixed permanently, that is, it was not to be increased ever in future." Zamindars collected rent from peasants and paid the Company. Problems: "the zamindars found it difficult to pay. Anyone who failed to pay the revenue lost his zamindari," while having no real incentive to improve the land itself — and "the rent [the peasant] paid to the zamindar was high and his right on the land was insecure."
Mahalwari System: developed by Holt Mackenzie in the North Western Provinces (1822) — revenue was assessed periodically, not fixed permanently, and collection responsibility fell to the village headman rather than a zamindar.
(Ryotwari system and the Santhal Rebellion specifically were not found in this chapter extract — worth a follow-up fetch since both are named BPSC syllabus lines.)

entries.heading: The National Movement (Class 8, "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947")
entries.text:
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): triggered by the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (April 1919) and the Khilafat agitation (Indian Muslims' anger at the harsh treaty imposed on the Turkish Sultan). "Thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges. Many lawyers such as Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, C. Rajagopalachari and Asaf Ali gave up their practices." Regional variants: Kheda (Gujarat) peasant campaigns against land revenue, coastal Andhra/Tamil Nadu liquor-shop picketing, Guntur "forest satyagrahas," Punjab's Akali gurdwara-reform alignment.
Civil Disobedience / Salt March (1930): Gandhi picked salt because "it was sinful to tax salt since it is such an essential item of our food" — a demand uniting rich and poor. The march covered 240 miles to Dandi, where marchers "broke the government law by gathering natural salt found on the seashore."
Quit India Movement (1942): Gandhi's "do or die" call resonated especially with peasants and youth. "Communications and symbols of state authority were attacked all over the country. In many areas the people set up their own governments." British repression: over 90,000 arrests and roughly 1,000 deaths by 1943.
